content: The Archaeplastida, also known as Primoplantae, represent a significant lineage of eukaryotic organisms. This group includes land plants, green algae, red algae, and a smaller group called glaucophytes. All members of this lineage possess plastids that are surrounded by two membranes, which strongly suggests that these plastids originated directly from endosymbiotic cyanobacteria. In contrast, plastids in other eukaryotic groups are surrounded by three or four membranes, indicating that they were acquired secondarily from green or red algae. Cells of Archaeplastida typically lack centrioles and contain mitochondria with flat cristae. Most of these cells have a cell wall composed of cellulose, and they store food in the form of starch. However, these features are not exclusive to Archaeplastida and are shared with other eukaryotes. Genetic studies provide the primary evidence that Archaeplastida form a monophyletic group, suggesting that plastids likely had a single evolutionary origin. Archaeplastida can be divided into two main evolutionary lineages. Red algae are characterized by their pigmentation, which includes chlorophyll a and phycobiliproteins, similar to cyanobacteria. On the other hand, green algae and land plants (collectively referred to as Viridiplantae, meaning green plants) are pigmented with chlorophylls a and b but lack phycobiliproteins. The phylogenetic position of glaucophytes remains uncertain. These organisms retain cyanobacterial pigments and are unique in preserving a peptidoglycan cell wall within their plastids, known as cyanelles. This feature is not found in other Archaeplastida. The term Plantae has historically been used to refer to this group, but its usage has been inconsistent, as it has also been applied to smaller clades such as Viridiplantae and embryophytes. To avoid ambiguity, alternative names have been proposed. The name Primoplantae was introduced in 2004, while the more precise term Archaeplastida was proposed in 2005 by Adl et al. All Archaeplastida possess plastids, commonly referred to as chloroplasts, which are responsible for photosynthesis. These chloroplasts are derived from cyanobacteria that were engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells. In glaucophytes, which are considered the most primitive members of this group, the chloroplasts (cyanelles) retain features of cyanobacteria, such as a peptidoglycan cell wall. This resemblance supports the endosymbiotic theory of plastid origin. Archaeplastida exhibit a wide range of cellular organization, from unicellular forms to filaments, colonies, and multicellular organisms. Multicellularity evolved independently in several lineages, including red algae, ulvophyte green algae, and the green algae that gave rise to stoneworts and land plants. Most Archaeplastida cells have cell walls, often composed of cellulose. The acquisition of chloroplasts in Archaeplastida occurred through a process known as primary endosymbiosis, where an ancestral eukaryote engulfed cyanobacteria. Evidence for this includes the presence of a double membrane around chloroplasts, with one membrane originating from the cyanobacterium and the other from the host eukaryote. Over time, many genes from the chloroplast were transferred to the host cell's nucleus. The presence of such genes in eukaryotes without chloroplasts suggests that this gene transfer occurred early in the evolution of Archaeplastida. Other eukaryotes with chloroplasts acquired them through secondary endosymbiosis, where a single-celled Archaeplastida with its own chloroplasts was engulfed by another eukaryote. For example, the chloroplasts of euglenids and chlorarachniophytes were derived from green algae, while those of heterokont algae, cryptophytes, haptophytes, and dinoflagellates were derived from red algae. These secondary endosymbiosis events resulted in chloroplasts surrounded by more than two membranes, reflecting their complex evolutionary history. The fossil record of Archaeplastida dates back to the Mesoproterozoic Era, approximately 1500 to 1300 million years ago. Microfossils from the Roper Group in northern Australia resemble modern green algae. These fossils align with molecular clock studies, which estimate that Archaeplastida diverged around 1500 million years ago. The oldest fossil that can be definitively assigned to a specific modern group is the red alga Bangiomorpha, dating to 1200 million years ago. During the late Neoproterozoic Era, algal fossils became more diverse and abundant. By the Paleozoic Era, plants had colonized land and have continued to thrive to the present day.
